newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil's Cardoso gambles to win re-election chance.
newsitem.headline: Brazil's Cardoso gambles to win re-election chance.

text.p: Brazil's president, Fernando Henrique Cardoso, spent Monday locked in talks with leaders of his multi-party alliance ahead of Tuesday's Congressional vote on a bill that would give him a chance to become the country's first re-elected leader.
Cardoso's goal, said analysts, was to make sure of the three-fifths majority the constitutional amendment needs for first approval of the bill in the Chamber of Deputies.

Officials made plans to borrow private jets to fly in sick deputies from around the country and hundreds of mayors began arriving in the Brazilian capital for a rally on Tuesday aimed at whipping up last-minute support for the bill, which would allow Cardoso to run for a second consecutive term.
"This is the big showdown. The president has used every last drop of his strength for this vote and I think he will win," said Paulo Kramer, a politics professor at Brasilia University.

If Congress approves the bill and his inflation-slashing policies stay on track, Cardoso would be hard to beat in the 1998 presidential race, Kramer said. "But without (the) re-election (bill) he might have trouble finishing his last two years," he added.
The re-election bill has to be approved twice in the two houses of Congress, each time by a 60 percent majority.

Government whips, who twice had to ditch attempts to vote on re-election earlier this month amid a rebellion among Cardoso's allies, said the vote might be put off until Wednesday but ruled out the chance of defeat.

"We're not talking about confidence any more; the word is certainty," Inocencio Oliveira, lower house leader of the government-allied Liberal Front Party, told reporters after meeting with Cardoso to discuss the bill's chances.

Brazil has prevented its presidents, state governors and mayors from seeking second consecutive terms since the founding of the republic in 1889. It wanted to prevent a repeat of the supreme powers enjoyed by the country's former Portuguese rulers.

But Cardoso says Brazil's newfound climate of low inflation and economic growth, which he introduced in 1994 when finance minister, needs the kind of political stability only his re-election could provide.

If successful, he would join presidents Carlos Menem and Alberto Fujimori of Argentina and Peru respectively as Latin American leaders who have rewritten their countries' constitutions to allow their own re-elections.
Cardoso's critics accuse the president of being obsessed with his political career at the expense of other reforms to streamline the state.
Ironically, the biggest threat to Cardoso's re-election plan has come from within his governing alliance.

Senior figures with the Brazilian Democratic Movement Party (PMDB), the biggest in Congress, insist the party can only vote on re-election after elections to choose the new presidents of the Chamber of Deputies and the Senate.

"At least half the PMDB's lawmakers won't show up for the vote," party's president Antonio Paes de Andrade told newswire Invest News before meeting with Itamar Franco, a former president who is considered a dark horse for the 1998 elections.
But most observers said the government had done enough to clinch victory in the Chamber of Deputies.
